I wouldn't fret too much about this stuff. It won't cause any slowdowns or anything like that if that's what you're thinking.

Clean? Remove packages I don't use. If my Arch computer hasn't been updated in a while and everything's stable I'll purge the old package backups before I upgrade. First time I did it I cleared out half the space on my root partition. Shit was nuts.

Snappy? I keep my memory and CPU usage to a minimum. I use i3 window manager instead of a desktop environment and don't include a lot of stuff to execute on login, just things like Redshift, Nitrogen, connman, etc. The only background applications I typically have running are xfce4-taskmanager, deadbeef, thunar, and xfce4-terminal. Removing packages doesn't really make it snappier unless you have a lot of auto-booting shit.

I rarely delete anything. Deleting old, "unneeded" files is a bad habit from the dark ages of low capacity platter based hard disks and fragmentful filesystems. If those files offend you so much, move them to external/offline storage.

It's different for everyone, but for me it was swimming up the delta to get as close to the kernel as comfortably possible. I'll never talk shit on these distros that are a fork of a fork of a fork, but at the end of the day fedora and debian (with the window manager of my choice) have always treated me best. Easier to troubleshoot, better documentation, etc.

TLDR: It's way better near the teet if you can invest some more time towards the learning curve.
I reinstall my os from scratch every so often.

Some Arch commends I use to clean up:

sudo pacman -Sc -- clearing pacman cache

sudo pacman-optimize -- optimizing pacman db

sudo pacman -Rsn $(pacman -Qqtd) -- removing unused package

Also, when I remove a package I always use pacman -Rsn instead of just pacman -R. It removes a package and its dependencies which are not required by any other installed package and prevents it from backing up configuration files when removing certain applications.
I'm not sure what the difference is but I do pacman -Scc

-Scc removes all the packages in the cache while -Sc keep the packages that are currently installed on the system. I prefer -Sc in case an update breaks something and I need to downgrade to the previous package.

Linux has a dozen or so different filesystems that could be used for storing the main install. All of them have very quick access time for filenames, so just having an un-used files or rarely used files isn't going to slow down much of anything. The exceptions to this is anything that will actually be accessed. Extra theme and media files slow down DEs, Icon files use resources, extra fonts are all indexed and use memory.

Beyond that, it isn't going to use much more than just space, which is the cheapest resource on most computers.

Well, I don't really know what to say. I'm really digging this site and feel that it definitely could be as strong and popular as Reddit someday, as long as the mods know better than to sell out the community for a PC website. I don't know what else to really talk about, so I thought I'd just share my journey of how I got to you awesome somebodies here at Voat.

With all this shit with Reddit being censored for sponsors and ads, I got to thinking about my internet future. I used to be a pretty active FaceBook user for awhile, constantly posting the latest links and news for everyone to see and (having had my account for years at this point) was getting a lot of traffic and "likes". It was the usual routine. Probably have been there before, yourself.

It wasn't until ads started popping up in the form of pages to be "liked" and "shared" that I was beginning to see the end of the FaceBook I had grown to love and use daily. Sure enough, I started losing interest; "liking" a post just to "like" it, but not actually gaining any value out of it. I would read the articles, finding as diverse sources as I could. But, alas, FaceBook (and Google) had kept up with my interests so long they were sharing and linking me to a select source group, not trusting that I may be a little adventurous and want the controversy or "devil's advocate" to whatever issue or subject I was looking up. This is when I discovered Reddit.

Reddit appeared so many times in just the past two years to me, I was astonished I had put it off for so long. Maybe because it was the "in" thing, and after seeing what most of the mainstream's effects on our society could do (i.e. FaceBook, Twitter, Tumblr), I was always hesitant to give it a try or invest in it. Or maybe it was my friends pressuring me to use it all the time, and I assumed they were just hyping it because it was something they knew that I didn't. However, one day I got adventurous enough and decided FaceBook didn't have all the information I could be getting. So, I took a little trip to Reddit.

I downloaded the app and was really impressed by it's organization (which I later learned the website has almost none of), detail to users and the community posting on it, and taken aback by just what sort of things could be viewed/posted/said on there without all hell and judgement being rained down (something I was treated to daily in FaceBook. "Controversial" views). It was nothing I had ever experienced before. And even learning later of the type of subverses that existed before the FBI got involved, really opened my eyes to the possibilities of the internet post-Patriot Act and just what sort of things could be done, good and bad. I was enthralled and quickly jumped aboard the S.S. Reddit, taken more in by not even having to register an email or anything. Completely anonymous to anyone I may know (lest they know my screen name)! I felt untethered by the normalcy of the standards of social media. Boy, I was naive...

Suddenly, /r/Gore is gone. Well, not gone, per se. Just hidden in a corner of the website, requiring an email and verification to subscribe.... which is odd and it struck me as such. Why would a sub that had been apart of Reddit since it's early days, suddenly be wiped off the face of the front page? And worse, why a need to register to be able to view that sub? That's when a rumor starting going around that Germany had something to do with /r/Gore's shut down.

How could that be, though? Well, when you want to sell something to the masses, you need to make sure it's actually suitable for the masses. So, when, oh let's say, extending on advertising and sponsors start being planned, things need to be reevaluated and reexamined to make sure everything looks nice and inviting to the new people looking to get in on the community. Sadly, that means making a lot of cool, Weasley-looking houses into mundane, white-picket-fence-four-member-family cul de sacs: boring, same, safe. As well as having your personal registration to something you may not want known to be involved or interested in. We all have those dark curiosities that beckon us to explore when we are vulnerable and in a position to do so.

Which brought me over to Voat. When I heard about this alternative to Reddit, I thought it was going to be some sort of cheap knock-off, skeletal Reddit. But, I am still being wow-ed at just how much it can stand on it's own. Yeah, it's not much and it certainly is a hell of a lot smaller than Reddit, but give it time. Reddit started off small, too. I think with a little time and patience this community will grow and get better and better.
